originalRequest: Produce the English variant of the shipped Chinese course learn-multi-agent-collaboration for learn.agentmentor.dev. Teaching rewrite in English (not a translation): same 6-lesson structure, same lesson slugs, same interactive-block ids and answer positions, source quotes restored to their verbatim English originals from sources.md, runnable code kept logic-identical with only comments and user-facing strings translated, cross-course references pointing at the live English course titles, natural desk-voice English prose with no AI-slop register.

briefCompleteness.evidence: The owner ratified the multilingual plan explicitly: all six locales on learn.agentmentor.dev, English first, batches of 2-3 courses in path order with a commit per course. The zh course is the verified source of truth for scope, learner model, structure, and grounding, so no additional clarification was needed.

learnerModel.targetReader: A developer who has finished the first five courses in this series, can write basic prompts, understands the tool-calling protocol, knows about agent memory and state, and can read basic JavaScript
knownConcepts: Basic JavaScript (variables, functions, async/await, array methods)
Running Node.js scripts in a terminal
That an agent reads context, decides, calls tools, and loops
unknownConcepts: When a task is worth splitting across multiple agents
The orchestrator-subagent architecture and context isolation
The pipeline, producer-reviewer, and voting patterns
Multi-agent failure modes (unverifiable 'done', duplicated work, conflicting results)
Defensive parsing of a reviewer's JSON output
learnerModel.assumedEnvironment: A Node.js environment, terminal access, a text editor, and a working Claude API key for the lesson 6 exercise
learnerModel.firstIndependentAction: Take a task they're considering handing to multiple agents and judge whether coordination overhead outweighs the benefit
noviceRamp: Lesson 1 motivates multi-agent work from the limits of a single context (pollution, attention dilution) before any architecture
Lesson 2 introduces orchestrator-subagent with context isolation and why a subagent returns only its conclusion
Lesson 3 teaches self-contained delegation prompts (objective, output format, tools, boundaries)
Lesson 4 contrasts pipeline / producer-reviewer / voting patterns and where each fits
Lesson 5 covers failure and coordination (the trust-then-verify gap) as a relatively independent unit, and lesson 6 builds a runnable producer-reviewer pipeline

learnerBrief: The target reader has finished the first five courses, writes basic prompts, understands tool calling and agent memory, and reads JavaScript. They don't yet know when or how to split work across agents. The course gets them to judge when multi-agent is worth it, apply the orchestrator-subagent architecture with context isolation, write self-contained delegation prompts, distinguish pipeline/producer-reviewer/voting patterns, recognize multi-agent failure modes and defenses, and finally build a runnable producer-reviewer pipeline with the Claude API.
scope: Covered: when splitting a task across agents is worth it and when coordination overhead wins, the orchestrator-subagent architecture and context isolation, fan-out and aggregate, self-contained delegation prompts, the pipeline / producer-reviewer / voting patterns, multi-agent failure modes (unverifiable 'done', duplicated work, conflicting results) and the trust-then-verify gap, result integration and citation attribution, token cost, and a runnable producer-reviewer pipeline. Not covered: the source code of multi-agent frameworks, distributed-systems consensus algorithms, or building a general-purpose orchestration platform from scratch. Depth: from zero to understanding the collaboration patterns and building a runnable two-agent pipeline.

qualitySelfReview.diagramUse: Diagrams are kept exactly where the zh original uses them (fan-out/aggregate and the collaboration-pattern shapes), with labels rewritten in English; none added or removed. Multi-agent topology is precisely the content a diagram conveys better than prose, and the zh placement was already review-validated.
weakestPoints: Lesson 4's pattern taxonomy (pipeline / producer-reviewer / voting) is a simplification; real systems combine them, noted where it matters
Lesson 1's token-cost figures (4x, 15x) are Anthropic's reported data for a specific system and are framed as such, not as universal constants
Lesson 6's pipeline is teaching-grade and single-run; it is explicitly not a production orchestration framework, and the reviewer JSON is defensively parsed rather than assumed valid

As an English teaching rewrite of a verified zh course, idiomatic drift is the residual risk: source quotes were restored verbatim from English originals and runnable code kept logic-identical, but prose was re-taught rather than translated, so review must check meaning-equivalence against the zh lessons

acceptanceReview.terminalTask: The learner can decide whether a task warrants multiple agents, write a self-contained delegation prompt with scope and output format, choose the fitting collaboration pattern, and build a runnable producer-reviewer pipeline with the Claude API that defensively parses the reviewer's JSON, verifies subagent claims rather than trusting them, and stops on a bounded loop.
acceptanceReview.interactionCheck: Six agentmentor-check blocks, one per lesson (when-to-split in L1, subagent-visibility in L2, vague-instruction in L3, pipeline-vs-reviewer in L4, trust-subagent in L5, invalid-review-JSON in L6), preserved from the zh variant with identical ids, modes, choice counts, and correct-answer positions; label, prompt, whyHere, choice text, and feedback are English teaching rewrites specific to each lesson's misconception. Exercises keep the zh Level structure with rubric, answer, and hints per Level.
acceptanceReview.learnerFitCheck: The course assumes the prior five courses, basic prompting, the tool-calling protocol, agent memory/state, and JavaScript reading. When to split, orchestration, delegation prompts, collaboration patterns, and the failure model are taught from zero in dependency order; the learner first builds a full pipeline in lesson 6, after every prerequisite. Lesson 1's first exercise asks only for a worth-it judgment on the reader's own task.
